name: Ace of Spades
creator_name: David Collyer (dressing shown by Paul Little, Flydresser Spring 2009)
description: A 1960s stillwater lure from Surrey with a black body, black hen hackles bound down Matuka-style, a guinea fowl throat and a bronze mallard roof over the top.
fishing_tips: Best on an intermediate line with long, slow draws or a slow figure-of-eight. If nothing follows, speed up. On a floater, add a little flat lead under the body and lengthen the leader.
mats: Long shank lure hook (e.g. Partridge Bomber), #8
steps: Start the thread a short way behind the eye and tie in the oval silver tinsel along the shank, taking the thread back to just short of the hook point.
Strip the fluff from a length of Vernille, tie it in at the rear and wind it forward as a smooth body, leaving room for the head. Strip the core at the tie-in point to keep the head slim.
Pair four hen hackles, two from each side of the cape so their curves match. Strip the underside fibres along the body length so they sit flat on the back.
Lay the hackles along the top of the body and bind them down Matuka-style with open turns of the rib, using a dubbing needle to free trapped fibres.
Now add a throat of guinea fowl about half the body length. (Adding the throat before the wing gets in the way of the rib, so do it here.)

Take a slip from a left-hand bronze mallard feather and set it on the near side with a loose pinch wrap, pulling the thread up slowly so the fibres don't crease. Repeat on the far side with a right-hand slip.
Trim the butts, build a neat head with flattened thread, whip finish and give it two coats of varnish.
imitates: Leech, fry or large dark nymph; a general stillwater lure
hatch: All season; best early spring and autumn on reservoirs

name: The Ackroyd (Waddington)
creator_name: Richard Waddington style, tied by Steve Silverio (Flydresser Spring 2020)
description: The classic Ackroyd dressed on Richard Waddington's 'Rational Fly' shank: a yellow-and-black body, a slim white bucktail wing and a treble hook held in line so the fly swims like a baitfish.
fishing_tips: A swimming salmon fly for higher water. Waddington tied his wings sparse and low along the body so the fly looks like small prey in the current.
mats: 25 lb monofilament (to lock the treble straight)
Rear half yellow seal's fur, front half black wool
Yellow body hackle; black heron or substitute at the front
Oval silver tinsel tag, yellow silk body
steps: Fix the Waddington shank in the vise. If you want the treble held rigid, bind a piece of 25 lb mono along the shank, leaving a tag end at the back.
Tie in the flat silver rib and the yellow body hackle at the rear. Dub the back half of the shank with yellow seal's fur and the front half with black wool, leaving room at the front.
Wind the body hackle forward in open turns, then follow it with the rib, each turn sitting just in front of a hackle turn.
At the front, wind two turns of the black heron (or substitute) hackle, then two turns of guinea fowl as a collar.
Add a slim wing of white bucktail lying low over the body, then a jungle cock feather on each side. Form a neat head, whip finish and varnish.
Dress the treble separately: a few touching turns of oval silver tinsel for the tag, then a smooth yellow silk body. Whip finish.
Slot the treble onto the shank. If you used mono, bind its tag end down just behind the body to keep the treble straight, then trim.

name: Alder Larva
description: A raggy brown-olive nymph with a split tail and a partridge hackle, the 'brown' cousin of a damsel nymph. Simple to tie and better the more chewed up it gets.
fishing_tips: Fish it slow and deep on a sinking line, especially early in the season. Keep a few weighted with fine lead wire for deeper water.
mats: Brown-olive seal's fur mix with some fluorescent fibres
steps: Lay a thread base and, if you want it weighted, add a few turns of fine lead wire.
Tie in the first hackle-tip tail. Make a small bump of dubbing and use it to splay the other two tails out sideways (optional; it fishes fine without).
Make a dubbing rope of the seal's fur mix and wind a shaggy, untidy body. Pick it out with a dubbing needle if it looks too neat.
Tie in a brown partridge hackle by its tip and wind two or three turns so the shorter fibres sit at the back.
Tie off, build a small head and whip finish.
imitates: Alder fly larva (Sialis lutaria) crawling ashore to pupate
hatch: Larvae all year; most active April–May before the adults emerge

name: Whiskey Fly
creator_name: Albert Willock (shown by Ian McKenzie, Flydresser Winter 2015)
description: A bright 1970s stillwater lure: silver body ribbed with fluorescent red, an orange throat and a hot orange calf tail wing. Rainbows still can't leave it alone.
fishing_tips: Strip it on a floating or intermediate line for stocked rainbows, especially in coloured water. Many small stillwaters limit lures to a size 10 long shank.
mats: Fluorescent red floss (Glo-Brite No. 4) or the red thread
Hard varnish or UV resin over the body
steps: Run the thread down to above the barb and tie in the fluorescent red floss.
Tie in the flat silver tinsel, take the thread back to the eye and wind a smooth tinsel body, leaving room behind the eye for the throat and wing.
Make a small butt with the floss, then rib it up the body and tie off. Coat the body with varnish or thin resin and let it set.
Tie in a throat of orange hackle fibres that just reaches the hook point.
Add a wing of hot orange calf tail, build a prominent red head, whip finish and varnish.
imitates: Attractor lure; suggests a small fry
hatch: Summer, especially when trout chase fry; works in bright conditions

name: Appetiser
creator_name: Bob Church, 1972 (shown by Ian McKenzie, Flydresser Winter 2015)
description: Bob Church's roach-fry lure from Grafham Water, one of the first patterns to use marabou: white chenille body, mixed green, orange and mallard tail and throat, white marabou wing under grey squirrel.
fishing_tips: Fish it where trout are chasing fry in late summer and autumn, with pulls and pauses so the marabou breathes.
mats: Mixed green and orange cock hackle fibres plus a few mallard flank fibres
White marabou topped with grey squirrel tail
steps: Take the thread to above the barb and tie in the mixed tail, then the oval tinsel and the chenille.
Return the thread behind the eye, leaving room for the hackle and wing. Wind the chenille body and rib it with the tinsel in the opposite direction. Tie off.
Tie in a beard of the same mixed fibres as the tail.
Strip the fluff from the base of a good bunch of white marabou and tie it in so it reaches just past the bend.
Add a small bunch of grey squirrel tail over the marabou, form the head and varnish.
imitates: Coarse-fish fry (roach and perch fry)
hatch: Late summer to autumn when trout feed on fry

name: Articulated Stonefly Nymph
creator_name: Sergio Córdoba, Argentina (Fly Dressers' Guild Pattern Library)
description: A semi-realistic, two-hook articulated stonefly nymph with a segmented vinyl abdomen, scud-back wing pads, silicone legs and epoxy eyes. The rear hook is cut off, leaving a hinged body that wiggles.
fishing_tips: Bounce it along the bottom of fast, rocky runs where big stoneflies live. Add weight in the eyes or body for deep water.
mats: #10 straight hook for the abdomen, #10 curved hook for the thorax
Yellow rabbit dubbing with a clear vinyl rib
Scud Back or other clear strip
Brown craft fur and yellow dubbing
steps: Taper short lengths of mono with a scalpel for the tails and antennae.
On the abdomen hook, tie in the two tails and colour them with a marker.
Tie in the vinyl rib, dub yellow rabbit to the eye, then wrap the vinyl forward in touching turns to make a segmented abdomen. Tie off and cut the hook off behind the body.
On the thorax hook, lay mono from the eye to the bend, thread it through the abdomen hook's eye and bring it back along the shank. Fold both ends back and bind them down so the joint is secure.
Tie a tuft of craft fur at the bend of the thorax hook, then tie in the three pairs of silicone legs and dub around the hind legs.
Cut the hind and fore wing pads from Scud Back. Tie the hind pad on top between the back two pairs of legs and colour it.
Dub around the middle legs, add a tuft of craft fur on top, then tie the fore wing pad between the middle and front legs with another small tuft of fur.
Tie in a strip of Scud Back at the base of the fur, tie the antennae in an X at the eye and dub behind them to build the head.
Pull the Scud Back forward over the front of the thorax and then the head, tying it down at each.
Shade the wing case, thorax, head, antennae and legs with markers. Kink the legs with a warm needle and build the eyes with epoxy.
imitates: Large stonefly nymph (Perlidae / Perlodidae)
hatch: Nymphs all year in rivers; most active before the spring and early-summer hatches

name: Atomic Anchovy
description: A saltwater anchovy with a pearl mylar body, white hair with blue and black flash, grizzly cheeks and an extended mylar hood over a cone head, finished with epoxy eyes.
fishing_tips: Fast strips around bait balls for bluefish, Spanish mackerel and jacks. The cone and epoxy head give it a darting, jiggy action.
mats: Cone head on a short piece of flared tube liner
Large pearl mylar tube, end sealed with a flame
steps: Lay a thread base. Slide a short piece of tube liner, flared at the eye end with a flame, onto the shank, push the cone over it and lock it with a drop of superglue.
Behind the cone, tie in a length of cored-out pearl mylar tube balloon-style for the body, with a touch of superglue at the rear tie-off.
Directly behind the cone, tie in fine white hair above and below the shank, then blue Krystal Flash and a little black Krystal Flash on top.
Tie a grizzly hackle on each side as a cheek, running the length of the body. Secure and glue the butts.
Cut a piece of wide pearl mylar tube that slips over the cone. Carefully seal the cut end with a flame so the strands fuse (mask the rest so it doesn't catch).
Cut it to about half the body length, tie it on in front of the cone with the sealed end facing forward, then roll it back over the cone to form an extended hood.
Colour the top of the hood with a black marker, add an eye on each side and coat the whole head with epoxy, turning it while it cures.

name: Ballinaroone
description: An Irish hairwing loosely based on the Green Butt: half fluorescent green, half black body, orange throat, black squirrel and green Krystal Hair wing with jungle cock. A clear-water fly.
fishing_tips: Made for low, clear water. It has taken fish when other patterns were refused, including on the Blackwater in September.
mats: Rear half fluorescent green floss, front half black floss
Orange cock hackle, as a beard
Black squirrel tail with a few strands of green Krystal Hair
steps: Lay a thread base and form a short silver tinsel tag at the rear.
Tie in a golden pheasant topping as the tail, then the rib.
Wind the rear half of the body in fluorescent green floss and the front half in black floss. Rib up the body and tie off.
Tie in an orange cock hackle beard.
Add a sparse wing of black squirrel with a few strands of green Krystal Hair, then a jungle cock cheek on each side.
Form a neat black head, whip finish and give it two coats of varnish.

name: Bibio Hopper
description: A stillwater hopper with a carrot-shaped seal's fur body in black, red and black, a stretched pearl rib, knotted pheasant tail legs and a black hackle. Also tie it in claret, black or fiery brown.
fishing_tips: Tie with a stiff cock hackle to fish dry, or a soft hen hackle to fish it wet or greased in the film. A summer favourite when trout look up.
mats: Seal's fur: black, red, black in equal parts
steps: Lay a thread base and tie in the pearl Mylar. Stretch it until it turns pearly blue (if yours snaps instead, use a stretchable Mylar).
Dub a carrot-shaped body that thickens toward the eye: black at the rear, red in the middle, black at the front.
Rib tightly with the Mylar, tie it off securely and fluff the fur out with a Velcro brush.
Tie six knotted pheasant tail legs on the underside so they reach just past the bend.
Tie in the hackle and make about six wraps. Form a neat head, whip finish and varnish.
imitates: Heather fly (Bibio pomonae) and other black terrestrials blown onto the water
hatch: Heather fly: August–September; a general hopper all summer

name: Black, Peacock & Coral Long-Tail Tadpole
description: A 'crossover' tadpole for days when neither all-coral nor all-black works: a long coral marabou tail, a weighted pearly cactus chenille body and a black hen hackle.
fishing_tips: Fish it deep and slow off a floating line on a very long leader (22–25 ft). Don't strike at plucks; let the trout take it properly. Great in summer with a breeze on the water.
mats: Coral marabou, a modest bunch, long
steps: Lay a solid base of waxed black thread.
Tie in a not-too-large bunch of coral marabou starting directly above the barb. Leave the tail long.
Make several turns of lead wire in the middle of the shank, leaving room behind the eye for the hackle.
Tie in the pearl cactus chenille at the rear and wind it forward toward the eye.
Wind four to six turns of a full black hen hackle, tie off and trim.
Make a small head and whip finish. (An unweighted version is worth trying too.)
imitates: Leech, damsel nymph or small fish; general stillwater lure
hatch: All season on stillwaters, especially early and late

name: Black Pennell
description: A classic loch and lake wet fly: slim black floss body, oval silver rib, golden pheasant tippet and topping tail, and a sparse black hackle with long fibres for movement.
fishing_tips: A top-dropper fly for loch-style drifts, especially in dark or windy conditions. Use a webby cock or soft hen hackle for fast streams.
mats: Golden pheasant tippet with a topping over it
Black floss, split to a single strand
Black cock with long fibres (or soft black hen)
steps: Lay a few close turns of thread and tie in the fine oval silver tinsel. Make a four-turn tag and leave the rest of the tinsel for the rib.
Tie in a few golden pheasant tippet fibres for the tail, with a topping on top of them. Bind the butts down neatly.
Split the black floss to a single strand and wind a slim, even body.
Rib forward with the tinsel in open, even turns to just behind the eye.
Choose a black hackle with fairly long fibres (short fibres look lifeless), make only three or four turns and tie off.
Form a small head and whip finish.
imitates: Hatching chironomid (buzzer) or small dark insect
hatch: April–September; best in buzzer hatches and dark conditions

name: Bloodworm (Single)
creator_name: Caroline Emmet (Fly Dressers' Guild Pattern Library)
description: A quick bead-head bloodworm made from a single furled strand of red Spanflex. Thin, wriggly and heavy enough to sit on the bottom.
fishing_tips: Fish it almost static over silty bottoms on stillwaters, or dead-drift it in rivers. Pale olive is a good alternative colour.
mats: Red Spanflex or Flexifloss (or pale olive)
steps: Slide the bead on, put the hook in the vise and start the thread right behind the bead with a narrow base of 2–3mm.
Tie in one strand of Spanflex on top of the shank, pushing its tip into the bead's hole for a neat start, and bind it down tightly.
Twist the Spanflex many times in one direction until it furls back on itself when folded. More twist makes a thinner, tighter body.
Fold it to length (¼ to ½ inch), secure the loose end at the base with a few tight turns, trim and whip finish.
If the body looks lumpy, untwist it slightly, run a needle between the strands while stretching them, then let it twist back.
imitates: Chironomid larva (bloodworm)
hatch: All year on stillwaters; feeds near the bottom in winter and spring

name: Bloodworm Cluster
creator_name: Caroline Emmet (Fly Dressers' Guild Pattern Library)
description: Several furled Spanflex bloodworms on one hook, behind and in front of a tungsten bead, optionally with peacock herl heads. A mouthful of wriggling larvae.
fishing_tips: Fish it nearly static on silty bottoms, or dead-drift it in rivers.
steps: Slide the bead on and push it toward the eye. Start the thread just in front of the bend and tie in the Spanflex.
Twist and furl one worm as for the single bloodworm and bind it at the base.
Move 3–4mm toward the eye, stretch the Spanflex and wind two or three touching turns, then furl another worm. Repeat for a third, ending around mid-shank.
Push the bead back against the last worm. Tie a new strand of Spanflex in front of the bead and make two or three more worms there. Whip finish.
For heads, untwist each worm a little, slip in a couple of peacock herls, let it spring back and trim the herl to 3–5mm.
imitates: A clump of chironomid larvae (bloodworms)
hatch: All year; most effective in cold water and early season

name: Parachute Bloodworm
creator_name: Caroline Emmet (Fly Dressers' Guild Pattern Library)
description: A floating bloodworm: a furled Spanflex worm hanging under a foam post and a sparse grizzly parachute, for trout picking larvae off the surface film.
fishing_tips: Fish it static in the film when trout are sipping near the surface.
mats: Dry fly hook (e.g. Partridge The Dry), #12–16
Thin foam cylinder or strip, up to 2mm
Grizzly, one size larger than the hook
steps: Start the thread 4–5mm behind the eye, tie in the Spanflex and furl a worm as for the single bloodworm. Tie it down tightly and trim.
Point one end of the foam and tie it in just in front of the worm as a post.
Tie in the grizzly hackle shiny side up and wind two to four sparse parachute turns.
Lock it: take the thread around the post twice near the hook, wrap once holding hackle and thread together, release and wrap again so the hackle pulls into place.
Whip finish under the parachute and trim the post to length.
imitates: Chironomid larva near the surface
hatch: Spring through autumn, when trout feed high

name: Brian's Fly
creator_name: Brian Leadbetter (shared by Chris Reeves, Fly Dressers' Guild Pattern Library)
description: A small palmered wet with a white fluorescent tail, near-black fiery brown seal's fur body, gold wire rib and a red game hackle. Brian Leadbetter's 'they're eating something, I don't know what' fly.
fishing_tips: A great middle fly on a washing-line rig on big reservoirs, especially on blustery days when fish are rising to who knows what.
mats: About 8 strands of white Glo-Brite floss (single strand)
Dark fiery brown seal's fur, almost black with an orange glint
Red game or ginger cock, palmered
steps: Lay a thread base and tie in a short tail of white fluorescent floss.
Tie in the gold wire and the red game hackle at the rear.
Dub a slim body of dark fiery brown seal's fur. Don't overdress it.
Palmer the hackle forward in open turns and tie it off.
Wind the wire back through the hackle, wiggling it side to side so you don't trap fibres. Tie off.
Add a couple of turns of brown hen at the head if you want more movement, then whip finish.
imitates: General attractor wet; suggests a small fish or nymph
hatch: All season

name: BugPole
description: A small weighted shrimp-style bug with a pearl shellback, a twisted copper rib and a squirrel or hare body. Built for grayling and nymphing chalkstream browns.
fishing_tips: Spot the fish, cast upstream and let it dead-drift. Any movement of the leader, or a fish shifting near the fly, means lift.
mats: Fine copper wire twisted into a rope
Dubbed squirrel or hare (or brown Microbrite)
steps: Tie in a short length of lead wire about 1mm behind the eye and bind down 8–9 turns.
Cut a 4mm strip of pearl sheet and tie it in at the tail.
A millimetre or two forward of the tail (so it can't slip off), tie in the twisted copper rib.
Dub hare or squirrel and make two turns behind the rib, then carry the body forward to the head.
Stretch the pearl strip over the back, tie it down and trim. Bring the rib forward and make two turns at the head.
Whip finish and coat the shellback with a heavy varnish.
imitates: Damsel nymph or small leech
hatch: May–September on stillwaters

name: Caperer Caddis
description: A semi-realistic tented-wing caddis using just four materials: a chunky snowshoe rabbit body, a CDC underwing for legs and float, a resin-stiffened mottled hen feather wing and deer hair horns. Change size and colour to match your local sedges.
fishing_tips: Tie it to match the Caperer that hatches in September, or your own local caddis. Caddis make up a big share of a trout's diet from April to October.
mats: Cinnamon or tan snowshoe rabbit dubbing
Mottled cinnamon hen saddle feather, coated with flexible UV resin
steps: Prepare the wing feathers ahead of time: run a drop of flexible UV resin along each side of a soft, mottled hen saddle feather and cure it. Trim the tip round if needed.
Start the thread at the eye and wrap back to the barb position.
Dub snowshoe rabbit loosely and heavily, and wind a chunky body over the rear two-thirds of the shank. (Turning the hook upside down keeps the point away from your fingers.)
Line up the tips of four CDC feathers and tie them on top so they reach just past the back of the hook.
Strip the lower fibres from a prepared wing feather so it reaches the back of the hook and the tie-in point is about a quarter of the feather's width.
Fold the feather down around the body like a tent with your fingers, make three wraps to curl it, then lock it with wraps under and over the tent. Trim the waste.
Tie in two deer hair fibres with their curve pointing up as horns.
Dub a heavy, cone-shaped head, putting the last wrap or two in front of the horns to stand them up. Whip finish twice (no varnish keeps it light).
imitates: The caperer sedge (Halesus radiatus), adult
hatch: Late August to October, evening hatches

name: CDC Black Pennell
description: The Black Pennell with two black CDC feathers in place of the hen hackle. The CDC holds air bubbles at first, then gives the fly lots of movement once it's wet.
fishing_tips: Fish it as you would a normal Black Pennell, on the top dropper in a wave.
steps: Lay a thread base and make a small red thread tag at the rear.
Tie in a few golden pheasant tippet fibres for the tail, then the oval silver rib.
Dub a slim body of black seal's fur and rib it with open turns of tinsel.
Wind two black CDC feathers as a hackle (if the stems are thick, put the fibres in a dubbing loop and wind that instead).
Form a small head and whip finish.
imitates: Hatching midge (buzzer) at the surface
hatch: April–September, especially evening buzzer hatches

name: CDC Mayfly Emerger
description: A traditional wet mayfly turned into an emerger: pheasant tail tail, olive seal's fur body, an olive CDC collar and a green-dyed French partridge front hackle. Fish it in the film, or sink it as a wet if nothing rises.
fishing_tips: Start it in the surface during a mayfly hatch. If it's ignored, pull it under and fish it as a wet fly with extra CDC movement.
steps: Lay a thread base and tie in a few cock pheasant tail fibres as the tail.
Tie in the fine silver wire, dub an olive seal's fur body to about three-quarters of the shank and rib it.
Wind an olive CDC feather as a collar.
Wind a green partridge hackle in front of the CDC.
Form a small head and whip finish.
imitates: Mayfly (Ephemera danica) emerging through the film
hatch: Late May to mid-June

name: CDC Yellow Hopper
description: A bright yellow hopper with a Pseudo Hackle body ribbed red, a yellow CDC wing, knotted pheasant tail legs set above the shank and a yellow cock hackle.
fishing_tips: A summer stillwater dry for trout taking terrestrials and hoppers.
mats: Knotted pheasant tail, tied above the shank
steps: Lay a thread base and tie in the red floss at the rear.
Wind a body of yellow Pseudo Hackle to about three-quarters of the shank and rib it with the floss.
Tie in a wing of yellow CDC on top.
Tie knotted pheasant tail legs along each side, set above the hook shank.
Wind a few turns of yellow cock hackle, form a head and whip finish.
imitates: Hatching midge or small sedge in pale colours
hatch: Summer, warm evenings

name: CDC Emerging Mayfly
description: An emerging mayfly with Coq de Leon tails, an olive seal's fur body, a pale olive CDC wing under a pheasant tail wing case, and a darker olive CDC hackle.
fishing_tips: Fish it in the surface film during the mayfly hatch, letting the CDC wing sit up.
mats: Light olive or yellow CDC feather
steps: Tie in a few Coq de Leon fibres as the tail and the silver wire rib.
Dub an olive seal's fur body and rib it.
Tie in a bunch of pheasant tail fibres for the wing case, then a light olive CDC feather as the wing.
Pull the pheasant tail forward over the base of the CDC wing and tie it down.
Wind two darker olive CDC feathers as a soft wet-fly hackle, form the head and whip finish.
imitates: Mayfly (Ephemera danica) emerger
hatch: Late May to mid-June

name: CDC Sedge
description: A palmered sedge with a fiery brown seal's fur body, a wing of two CDC feathers back to back, a brown cock collar and mallard flank antennae.
fishing_tips: Skate or twitch it across the surface on summer evenings when sedges are hatching.
mats: Two CDC feathers back to back
steps: Tie in the wire rib and a brown saddle hackle at the rear.
Dub a fiery brown seal's fur body, palmer the hackle forward and rib through it with the wire.
Place two CDC feathers back to back and tie them in flat over the body as the wing.
Wind a brown cock collar hackle in front of the wing.
Tie in two mallard flank fibres as antennae, form the head and whip finish.
imitates: Adult caddis (sedge)
hatch: May–September, evenings

name: Copper Bugger
description: A brown alternative to the black, white and olive Woolly Bugger: copper bead, long brown marabou tail with Krystal Flash, brown chenille body and a soft brown hackle wound from the head back and locked with gold wire.
fishing_tips: Works on any line, but best off an intermediate with an 18 ft leader and a slow retrieve. Don't strike at plucks on the long tail; keep the retrieve coming until the fish commits.
mats: Brown marabou, generous, with Krystal Flash each side
steps: Thread the bead on with the countersunk hole facing the eye, make a few thread turns behind it and add several turns of lead wire (glue the bead with superglue).
Tie in a generous bunch of brown marabou at the tail and bind it down firmly. Add two or three strands of Krystal Flash on each side.
Tie in the fine gold wire, then the chenille, and wrap the chenille forward to just behind the bead.
Catch in the brown hackle by the stalk behind the bead, make a couple of turns there, then spiral it back toward the bend.
Trap the hackle tip with the gold wire at the bend, then wind the wire forward through the hackle in open turns to the bead.
Secure the wire with a couple of thread turns, trim and whip finish behind the bead.
imitates: Leech, crayfish or large nymph
hatch: All season; best in cooler months

name: Cormorant
creator_name: Chris Reeves (Fly Dressers' Guild Pattern Library)
description: A slim, simple black fly with a peacock herl body, copper wire rib and a wisp of black marabou wing. Designed to hang on a washing-line rig during a buzzer hatch.
fishing_tips: Fish it as the middle dropper on a washing-line rig. Keep the wing sparse: once it gets bulky it's just another black lure. Variations use a pearl Mylar body or red or green holographic ribs.
steps: Cover the shank with thread from the eye to the start of the bend.
Tie in the copper wire along the length of the body.
Tie in two or three peacock herls (cut off the weak last 2cm of the tips) and wind a neat body, side by side or twisted into a rope. Trim.
Rib with the wire. Wind it the same way as the herl to hide it, or the opposite way to make it stand out.
Tie in a slim wing of 10–15 strands of black marabou at the head.
Form a small neat head, whip finish and varnish.
imitates: Damsel nymph, corixa or small fry; general stillwater wet
hatch: All season on stillwaters

name: Cosseboom
creator_name: John C. Cosseboom, Rhode Island (Flydresser Spring 2011)
description: The classic American salmon fly that began as a streamer: olive green floss body with an embossed silver rib, grey squirrel wing, lemon yellow collar and red head. The Flydresser article shows how much the look changes with the hook: long-shank streamer, old salmon iron, curved Bartleet or silver Salar.
fishing_tips: A dependable 'change' fly for salmon on both sides of the Atlantic; tie it small for trout. Pick the hook style to suit the water: straight long shank for a streamer, curved Bartleet for a classic salmon profile.
mats: Short tuft of olive green floss
steps: Lay a thread base and make a short tag of embossed silver tinsel.
Tie in a short tuft of olive green floss as the tail, then the tinsel for the rib.
Wind a smooth olive floss body and rib it with the tinsel.
Tie in a wing of grey squirrel tail lying low over the body.
Wind a lemon yellow hackle as a collar and sweep it back.
Build a neat red head, whip finish and varnish.

name: Cove's Pheasant Tail Nymph
creator_name: Arthur Cove (shown by Chris Reeves, Fly Dressers' Guild Pattern Library)
description: Arthur Cove's early buzzer: a pheasant tail body with a silver wire rib, a pheasant tail wing case and a rabbit or hare thorax. It passes for a big midge, a sedge pupa or even small fry.
fishing_tips: Fish it slowly on stillwaters during midge hatches. Try a seal's fur thorax or different body colours for variety.
steps: Start the thread behind the eye and form a neat underbody.
On the bend, tie in four pheasant tail fibres (more on bigger hooks; trim off the weak tips first) and the silver wire.
Wrap the pheasant tail forward in touching turns to the thorax and remove the waste.
Rib forward in even turns the opposite way to strengthen the body, then break off the excess wire.
Tie in six to eight pheasant tail fibres by the butts on top of the thorax area.
Dub a tight thorax of hare or rabbit (you can tease it out later for legs).
Pull the wing case forward, tie it down at the eye and trim. Whip finish and varnish.
imitates: Chironomid pupa (buzzer) or general nymph
hatch: April–October on stillwaters

name: Dafydd Lloyd
creator_name: Traditional Welsh pattern from Plu Stiniog (Flydresser Autumn 2010)
description: One of the oldest flies of the Ffestiniog quarry district in Wales: a cream-yellow silk body banded with gold, a red cockerel hackle and an unusual mixed wing of dark and grey mallard.
fishing_tips: A daytime fly for August and September when crane flies are blown onto the water in a stiff wind. Fish it on the point.
imitates: Crane fly (daddy-long-legs, family Tipulidae), adult blown onto the water
hatch: Late summer, especially August–September, on windy days when crane flies emerge from grassland
mats: Gold thread, tight turns as wide as the silk bands
Mixed dark and grey mallard fibres
steps: Lay a thread base and tie in the gold thread at the rear.
Wind a cream-yellow silk body, then rib it with tight turns of gold so the gold and silk bands look equally wide.
Wind a few turns of medium red cockerel hackle at the front.
Mix fibres of dark and grey mallard together and tie them in as a single wing over the body.
Form a small head and whip finish.

name: Dawson's Olive
description: A stillwater leech from Tunstall Reservoir: amber marabou tail, glazed olive chenille body with an oval silver rib, guinea fowl throat and an olive marabou wing reaching halfway down the tail. A 24 lb rainbow fell to one in 1992.
fishing_tips: Fish it with a jerky figure-of-eight to copy a swimming leech. For a bottom-crawl, add two or three layers of lead strip on top of the shank so it swims hook-up. A couple of thread wraps around the marabou base stops the tail fouling.
imitates: Leech (Hirudinea), swimming adult
hatch: All season; leeches are active from spring to late autumn and most important in coloured or weedy stillwaters
mats: Glazed olive chenille (or light olive Flash Bright dubbing)
Olive marabou, reaching halfway down the tail
Lead strip on top of the shank (optional)
steps: Start the thread behind the eye and wind in open turns to above the barb.
Tie in a generous spray of amber marabou for the tail. Pinch it to length rather than cutting.
In front of the tail, tie in the oval silver rib and the chenille. Strip a little fluff from the chenille end and tie in only the core to keep the body slim.
Take the thread to just short of the eye, wind the chenille body, then rib it with evenly spaced turns and tie off underneath.
Turn the fly over and tie in a false hackle of guinea fowl fibres.
Tie in the olive marabou wing so its tips reach halfway down the tail. Form a well-proportioned black head, whip finish and varnish twice.

name: One-Eyed Deer Hair Fry
description: A floating pinfry of spun and clipped white deer hair, coloured with markers, with a grey rabbit tail and one stick-on eye. It lies on its side like a stunned fry, so there's no eye on the side facing the sky.
fishing_tips: Fish it on the point of a washing-line rig when trout are hitting fry at the surface. It should only just float; squeeze it to push out water, and add floatant along the top.
imitates: Perch or roach fry (pinfry, 15–30 mm), stunned or dying at the surface
hatch: Mid-summer into autumn (June onward) when shoals of perch and roach fry gather in the margins
mats: Nymph hook, #6–10 to match the fry
Small bunch of grey rabbit guard hairs
White deer hair, spun and clipped
Grey, olive, black and red marker pens
steps: Tie in a small bunch of grey rabbit guard hairs as the tail.
Spin bunches of white deer hair along the shank as you would a muddler head, packing each one tight against the last with a pen tube.
Whip finish, then clip the hair into a slim fry shape.
Colour the back and sides with grey, olive and black markers and add a touch of red at the gills.
Stick an eye on one side only and work flexible superglue into the hair around it.

name: Foam-Backed Fry
description: A simple, very effective floating fry: a silver fritz body under a white foam back with a V-notched tail.
fishing_tips: Fish it alone or on the point when trout are chasing pinfry near the top. It's quick to tie and easy to replace.
imitates: Perch or roach fry (pinfry) near the surface
hatch: Mid-summer into autumn (June onward) when shoals of perch and roach fry gather in the margins
mats: Strip of white ethafoam, V-notched at the tail
steps: Start the thread at the bend and leave a few inches of the tag end hanging there; you'll use it to tie down the foam.
Tie in the foam strip at the bend, then the silver fritz, and wind the fritz forward to the eye.
Pull the foam over the back and tie it down at the head.
Use the hanging thread tag to bind the foam down at the bend, whip finish it there and cut a V in the foam tail.
Whip finish at the head and varnish both ends.

name: Mini Zonker
description: A small silver fritz body with a grey or white rabbit strip back held down by turns of silver wire. A tough little fry for when trout won't come up.
fishing_tips: Fish it on an intermediate line on bright, windy days when fry feeders stay below the surface.
imitates: Small fry or minnow, swimming
hatch: Mid-summer into autumn (June onward) when shoals of perch and roach fry gather in the margins
mats: Grey or white rabbit zonker strip
steps: Tie in the silver wire and the fritz at the bend, and wind the fritz forward to the eye.
Wet the rabbit strip and comb the fur upward with a toothbrush so it parts easily.
Tie the strip in at the head, lay it along the back and secure it at the bend.
Part the fur with a needle and bind the strip down with four or five turns of the wire up the body.
Tie off the wire at the head and whip finish.

name: Del Fatti's Mayfly
description: A natural-looking mayfly dun with a detached foam body made on a needle, moose tails, dun and olive hackles clipped flat underneath and wings of burned mallard or yellow-dyed elk. It lands right side up and floats well.
fishing_tips: For a true mayfly hatch on rivers and lakes. The elk hairwing version is the one Pat says really works, and it won't twist your leader like burned wings can in big sizes.
imitates: Mayfly (Ephemera danica), sub-imago dun
hatch: Late May to mid-June ('duffer's fortnight'), mostly afternoons and evenings
mats: Chinese cock, grey dun and light olive
Mallard flank (burned to shape) or yellow-dyed elk hair
steps: Cut a foam strip 5–5.5mm wide and cut half its width away along 30–35mm.
Put a long needle in the vise with 30–35mm sticking out and start the thread on it.
Tie the narrow part of the foam to the needle in open spirals, not too tight, then tie in three moose hairs for tails. Spiral the thread down and add glue.
Wind the wide part of the foam back over it, each wrap half covering the last (about ten wraps). Tie it down and tie off.
Gently push the finished body off the needle without crushing it, let the glue dry and colour it with markers.
Put a hook in the vise, cover the shank with thread and dub a small ball at the rear. Tie the body on with tight wraps, trim and cover the join with dubbing.
Tie in both hackles by their tips, crease the fibres back by running a scissor edge along the stems, wind them and cover with a little dubbing to make a shoulder.
Burn two mallard feathers to wing shape (or tie in a bunch of yellow elk). Tie them in with the good sides facing each other so they flare apart.
Bind the wing stalks tight, dub over them, clip the hackle flat underneath and whip finish.

name: Diawl Bach
creator_name: Traditional Welsh pattern (Malcolm Price, Fly Dressers' Guild Pattern Library)
description: The 'little devil': a single peacock herl body with a copper rib, a red game tail and throat. Simple, slim and one of the most reliable stillwater flies there is.
fishing_tips: Fish it slowly on a floating or midge-tip line, on its own or on a washing-line rig, whenever buzzers are about on reservoirs.
imitates: Chironomid midge pupa (buzzer), ascending to the surface
hatch: All season on stillwaters, peaking April–June and again in September; best in calm mornings and evenings
mats: Standard wet fly or nymph hook, #10–16
10–12 red game cock fibres, as long as the body
10–12 red game cock fibres, reaching the hook point
steps: Start the thread near the eye and run it back in touching turns to just short of the bend.
Tie in 10–12 red game fibres for a tail as long as the body, binding the butts along the shank for a smooth underbody.
Tie in the copper wire just behind the eye and bind it down along the shank to the tail.
Tie in one peacock herl by the tip (cut off the weak last inch) and wind it forward in touching turns to the eye.
Rib forward in open turns the opposite way to the herl, tie off and break off the waste.
Tie in a throat of 10–12 red game fibres that reach the hook point. Neaten the head, whip finish and varnish.

name: Flank Feather Shadow Mayfly
creator_name: Geoff Wilcox (Fly Dressers' Guild Pattern Library)
description: A one-feather emerger: a teal or mallard flank feather forms the tail, body and wing, with a few turns of peacock herl at the thorax. The grub hook hangs through the film while the body sits on it.
fishing_tips: Fish it as an emerging dun when fish are taking just under the surface. Trim the underside so it sits upright; too tall and it falls on its side.
imitates: Mayfly or large olive (Ephemeroptera) emerging through the surface film
hatch: Late spring through summer; olives April–October, true mayfly late May–June
mats: One teal or mallard flank feather
Cock hackle about 2.5× the hook gape
steps: Tie on a short bed of thread, about 4mm long.
Strip the fluff from a flank feather. Holding it by the tip, stroke about three-quarters of the fibres back; the tip becomes the tail.
Pinch the stroked feather to set the tie-in point and fix it to the hook with two pinch-and-loop wraps.
Lift the tail and body and put two turns behind; lift the wing and put two turns in front, so the feather is split into body and wing.
Stand the stem upright and lock it with a couple of wraps, smoothing the fibres back.
Tie in a peacock herl, wind four turns as a thorax and tie off.
Trim the wing, body and tail to shape. (Variant: use a smaller feather and wind a cock hackle through the split wing, two turns behind and two in front, then trim it flat underneath.)

name: Geert's Shrimp
hook_sizes: #2 (works larger or smaller, singles, doubles or trebles)
description: A two-part orange salmon shrimp with wood duck and golden pheasant feelers, a four-strand twisted gold and copper rib, yellow-dyed badger hackles and an orange collar.
fishing_tips: A bright shrimp for salmon in coloured or falling water. If you fish a Turle knot, leave room at the eye.
mats: Salmon single, heavy or standard iron, #2
White 8/0, then red for the head
Wood duck feather and a golden pheasant tippet
Two fine oval gold tinsels and two fine orange copper wires twisted into a rope
Orange fur (raccoon underfur or seal's fur), two sections
steps: Cover the hook point with a bit of clear tubing to save your fingers. Wind a copper wire tag to just above the point.
In front of the tag, wind a wood duck feather, folding the fibres back as feelers. Cut a V in a short golden pheasant tippet and tie it on top so it frames the tail. Keep both waste ends.
Bind the waste ends along the shank into a smooth underbody tapering toward the eye, stopping well short of it.
Tie in the twisted four-strand rib, dub orange fur over the rear half and make three even turns of rib. Tie off.
Fold a yellow badger hackle and wind two turns, sweeping the fibres back.
Dub the front half, rib it the same way and wind two turns of orange hackle as a collar.
Switch to red thread, wind two turns of a second yellow badger hackle in front, then form a neat head, whip finish and varnish.

name: Glass Bead Buzzer
description: A buzzer whose body is made of clear glass beads separated by thin rings of red or black Larva Lace, with a silver-lined orange bead behind a black metal head and white breathers. Ready-made segmentation and translucency with no epoxy.
fishing_tips: Fish it very slowly; takes are gentle and often come on the drop. For fishing near the surface, swap the metal head for a small black glass bead.
imitates: Chironomid midge pupa (buzzer), ascending or hanging in the film
hatch: Nearly year-round on stillwaters, heaviest April–June and September; calm, mild mornings and evenings
mats: Body colour of your choice; ultra-fine mono for the tail
Silver-lined orange bead behind the head, then clear glass beads
Red or black Larva Lace cut into fine rings
steps: Tie in the white breathers at the eye with figure-of-eight wraps.
Cover the body area with thread in your chosen body colour.
Slide on the metal head bead, the orange bead and then clear beads, with thin Larva Lace rings between them, setting them into wet varnish to brighten the colour.
Tie in a short tail of fluorescent white floss at the rear using fine mono thread.
Give the whole body one coat of clear varnish. The segmentation fades at first and returns as the varnish dries.

name: Gold Head Blue Flash Damsel
creator_name: Richard Ellis (Fly Dressers' Guild Pattern Library)
description: A weighted gold-head damsel with an olive marabou tail and blue mirror flash, a tapered olive rabbit body ribbed with gold wire and a green partridge hackle.
fishing_tips: Fish it with a slow figure-of-eight around weed beds and margins in late spring and summer, when damsel nymphs swim to shore to hatch.
imitates: Damselfly nymph (Zygoptera), swimming toward the margins to emerge
hatch: Late May through August, most active on warm, sunny days
mats: Olive marabou with 4 strands of blue mirror flash
Olive rabbit fur or damsel dubbing
steps: Slide the gold bead on (a slightly small bead keeps it from dominating) and add six turns of fine lead behind it.
Tie in a marabou tail just ahead of the bend, about 1.5 times the body length. Bind the butts down.
Tie in four strands of blue mirror flash at the same point, trimmed to the end of the marabou, and the gold wire.
Dub a body that tapers from slim at the rear to the diameter of the bead.
Rib forward in five open turns to the bead and break off the excess.
Wind one or two turns of green partridge, sweeping the fibres back so they reach the hook point. Whip finish behind the bead.

name: Green Machine
description: Warren Duncan's Miramichi bug: a silver tag, fluorescent green and red butt, Krystal Flash tail and a spun, clipped deer hair body with a palmered hackle drawn into it.
fishing_tips: A famous Miramichi salmon fly that works wherever anglers are brave enough to try it.
mats: White to start, strong GSP or Kevlar for spinning, then head colour
Fluorescent green floss and fluorescent red wool
12mm of silicone tube (to protect the tail while trimming)
steps: With white thread, wind a fine oval silver tag ending in line with the point. Lay a 4mm bed of thread in front of it.

Tie in two strands of green floss trailing back over the tag and one strand at the front. Build a green butt with them, then tie in fluorescent red wool and wrap it over the front part so green and red end up equal. Trim but keep the thread.
Tie in a small bunch of Krystal Flash in front of the butt, reaching the bend, and cut away the white thread.
Start strong GSP or Kevlar thread. Strip 12mm of fibres from the butt of a short saddle hackle and anchor the bare stem firmly.
Slide a 12mm piece of silicone tube over the tail, tag and hackle stem to protect them.
Spin small bunches of combed deer hair one at a time, compressing each firmly back (six to eight bunches), stopping 1.5–2mm from the eye.
Trim the hair roughly all round, then fine-tune the shape. Slide the silicone tube off.
Change to your head thread colour and wind the hackle forward in open turns, pulling it down into the clipped body. Make one extra turn, tie off, trim and varnish.

name: Hare Hackle Nymph
description: A weighted hare's fur nymph with lemon wood duck tails, a gold oval rib and a 'hackle' made of hare guard hair spun in a dubbing loop. The hackle outlasts everything else on the fly.
fishing_tips: A general-purpose buggy nymph for rivers and stillwaters. Fish it dead-drift or with a slow figure-of-eight.
imitates: General nymph: olive, sedge or stonefly nymph in drab colours
hatch: All season; most useful from spring through autumn before and during hatches
mats: Lemon wood duck or mandarin flank fibres
Hare's fur, mixed guard hair and underfur
Hare guard hair spun in a dubbing loop
steps: Lay a thread base and tie in a short tail of lemon wood duck fibres at the bend.
Tie in the rib, then the lead and wind it forward in touching turns, stopping 1.5–2mm from the eye to leave room for the hackle.
Dub a hare's fur body over the lead and pick it out with a needle if you like.
Rib forward in open, even turns to the end of the body.
Comb the underfur out of a pinch of hare body fur, leaving mostly guard hair. Make a dubbing loop and set the guard hairs in it at right angles with the tips level.
Spin the loop, wet it and stroke the fibres back, then wind it as a hackle, folding the fibres back with each turn. Tie off, whip finish and varnish if you like.

name: Halfback
description: A legendary buggy nymph from the North Platte River and Henry's Lake: pheasant tail tail and half-shell over two sections of peacock herl, each palmered with red-brown hackle.
fishing_tips: Dead-drift it upstream in rivers (unweighted sinks readily), or fish it unweighted on a sinking line in stillwaters.
imitates: General nymph: dragonfly, damsel or large mayfly nymph
hatch: All season; especially good in spring and early summer
mats: Red-brown cock saddle (or two neck hackles)
steps: Start the thread mid-shank, run it to the bend and tie in a bundle of pheasant tail half as long as the shank.
Wrap forward over the fibres a few turns, then fold them back and wrap rearward so the butts point to the tail (they'll become the shell).
Tie in a saddle hackle by the butt and a bundle of peacock herl by the tips. Twist the herls with the thread into a rope and wrap it to mid-shank.
Palmer the hackle to mid-shank and secure it with a few turns without trimming.
Pull the pheasant tail butts over the back of the rear body, tie them down and trim.
Make another herl rope and wrap it to one eye-width from the eye. Palmer the rest of the hackle over it, tie off, form a head and whip finish.

name: Hot Spot Corixa
description: A plump corixa with a thick cream floss body ribbed silver, a pheasant tail back and a red thread thorax as a hot spot.
fishing_tips: Fish it in shallow margins and over weed beds with short pulls and pauses, letting it rise and dive like a water boatman going up for air.
imitates: Corixa (lesser water boatman, family Corixidae), adult swimming
hatch: All year in stillwaters; most important late summer through winter in the shallows
steps: Lay a thread base and make a small oval silver tag, keeping the tinsel for the rib.
Tie in a bunch of pheasant tail fibres at the bend for the back.
Build a thick, plump body of cream floss and rib it with the silver tinsel.
Pull the pheasant tail over the back and tie it down behind the eye.
Build a small red thread thorax as the hot spot, whip finish and varnish the head.

name: Hydro Fly
description: A Scottish hairwing in an unusual colour mix: blue tinsel body ribbed silver, gold tag, topping tail, red wool butt, orange and guinea fowl hackles, and grey squirrel veiled with blue squirrel.
fishing_tips: A salmon and sea trout fly. Add jungle cock cheeks for brighter conditions.
mats: Soft orange cock, then guinea fowl
Grey squirrel under blue-dyed grey squirrel
steps: Wind a short tag of fine oval gold tinsel and tie in a small golden pheasant topping as the tail.
Make a small butt of red wool.
Tie in the oval silver rib under the shank at the butt, and the blue tinsel a few millimetres behind the eye. Wind the tinsel back to the butt and forward again, then secure it.
Rib forward and tie off under the shank.
Wind two or three turns of a soft orange hackle, then two turns of guinea fowl. Wet your fingers and stroke the hackles down under the shank.
Tie in a small bunch of grey squirrel no longer than the bend, with a slightly smaller bunch of blue squirrel over it to veil the top and sides.
Add jungle cock cheeks if you like, form the head and varnish twice.

name: Invicta
description: A century-old classic: golden pheasant topping tail, yellow seal's fur body palmered with red cock and ribbed gold, a blue jay beard and a hen pheasant tail wing. A fine test of tying order.
fishing_tips: From early season into April, pulled through the water it gets trout chasing with a bow-wave. A great sedge-pupa suggestion all summer on lochs.
imitates: Emerging sedge (caddis) pupa, swimming up to hatch
hatch: Sedges hatch from spring to autumn; the Invicta shines early season and on summer evenings
mats: Hen pheasant centre tail (two slips or one rolled slip)
steps: Lay a thread base and tie in the gold tinsel and a curved golden pheasant topping at the bend.
Dub a yellow seal's fur body, leaving plenty of room at the head for two hackles and a wing.
Tie in a red cock hackle at the front and palmer it back to the bend in open turns. Catch it with two turns of the rib.
Rib forward through the hackle to the front, then trim the hackle tip, butt and spare rib.
Turn the hook over, tie in a small bunch of jay fibres with level tips as a beard, and spread them evenly with your thumbnail.
Prepare hen pheasant tail slips (stroke the pointed tips down) and set them with a pinch-and-loop wrap, slightly long.
Trim the butts, form a small head and varnish. Shorten the wing by pinching with your fingernails, never scissors.

name: Leadhead
description: A deep-water nymph with a lead-free shot clipped onto mono at the head, a fluorescent green butt, a rabbit fur body and a speckled partridge collar. The shot makes it trundle along the bottom.
fishing_tips: Bounce it through the deepest runs and pools. The fluorescent green butt beat every other colour in testing. Use lead-free shot or a heavy bead where lead is banned.
imitates: Caddis larva or general nymph tumbling near the bottom
hatch: All season; deadly in cold early-season water and for grayling in winter
mats: Lead-free split shot pinched onto 0.3mm mono
Speckled brown partridge, wound as a collar
steps: Pinch a lead-free shot onto a short length of 0.3mm mono.
Tie the mono on top of the shank so the shot sits just behind the eye, and bind it down firmly.
At the rear, make a short butt of fluorescent green floss.
Dub a rabbit fur body forward to the shot.
Wind a speckled partridge hackle as a collar behind the shot, tie off and whip finish.

name: Marabou Damsel
description: A damsel made almost entirely of marabou: a long olive tail, a twisted-marabou body ribbed silver, a brown marabou back and a teased-out olive thorax behind a gold bead.
fishing_tips: Fish it slowly around weed beds and margins. Make the thorax about half the length of the body.
imitates: Damselfly nymph (Zygoptera), swimming
hatch: Late May through August, on warm sunny days
steps: Slide on the bead, secure it with thread and a little varnish, and run the thread to opposite the barb.
Tie in a bunch of olive marabou leaving about two inches as tail, and a 10cm length of silver tinsel.
Take the thread halfway to the bead. Twist the marabou into a tight rope, wrap it to the thread and tie off. Rib with four or five open turns.
Tie in a bunch of brown marabou on top and a smaller bunch of olive marabou.
Twist the olive into a rope and wrap a fatter thorax up to the bead. Pull the brown marabou over the top and tie it off at the bead.
Whip finish, varnish, tease out the thorax with Velcro and pinch the tail to length.

name: Thunder & Lightning (Spey variant)
creator_name: Anders Ståhl, Sweden (Fly Dressers' Guild Pattern Library)
description: A Spey-style fishing version of the classic Thunder and Lightning: gold and orange tags, black Antron body, orange palmered Spey hackle, blue shoulder and guinea fowl, and humped bronze mallard wings. Tougher and cheaper than the full dressing.
fishing_tips: A must in several sizes. Anders has caught salmon, coho, sea trout, rainbows, browns, perch, pike and grayling on it. Leave room at the eye for a Turle knot.
mats: Oval gold tinsel #14, then orange or red Antron (halved)
Heron, pheasant or schlappen dyed orange
Heron, pheasant or schlappen dyed blue, a little longer
steps: Above the hook point, wind three turns of oval gold tinsel, then a second tag of a few turns of orange Antron.
Tie in the gold rib and take the thread to the eye.
Prepare the orange body hackle: fibres as long as the shank, doubled (strip one side of a schlappen so it isn't bulky).

Tie in black Antron a few mm behind the eye and wind it back to the tag in diagonal touching turns. Come forward about 3mm and use it to trap the hackle tip, then wind an even, tight body to a few mm short of the eye.
Rib forward in five open turns, then wind the body hackle forward in five turns, each tucked just behind a tinsel turn. Tie off.
Wind two or three turns of the blue shoulder hackle, then three or four turns of doubled blue guinea fowl.
Cut four bronze mallard slips (two left, two right), hump each to follow the shank, and tie two stacked slips on each side.
Trim, shape a neat head, put a drop of superglue on it and varnish.

name: Muddler Minnow
description: The original that spawned countless variants: oak turkey tail and wing over a flat gold body with an oval rib, a grey squirrel underwing, and a spun, clipped deer hair head with a collar of hair tips.
fishing_tips: Strip it as a sculpin or minnow, swing it in rivers, or skate it on the surface. Works on almost any species that eats small fish.
imitates: Sculpin, minnow or small baitfish; skated, a hopper or caddis
hatch: All season; baitfish patterns shine from late summer into autumn
mats: Black or tan; strong thread for spinning
Oak mottled turkey quill slip, about 6mm
Oak mottled turkey quill slips, slightly wider
Natural deer hair, spun and clipped
steps: Start the thread about a third of the shank back from the eye and lay a smooth base to the bend.
Tie in a 6mm turkey slip as the tail, binding the butts along the shank to your starting point. Catch in the oval gold rib.
Tie in flat gold tinsel at the front, wind it to the bend and back, then rib forward in even open turns. Keep the underlayer flat so the tinsel stays smooth.
At the same front point, tie in a small bunch of grey squirrel as an underwing, then a pair of slightly wider turkey slips on top. Varnish the tie-in.
Clean and stack a small bunch of deer hair and tie it in holding the tips, so they point back to form the collar.
Spin four or five more small bunches to fill the front of the shank, compressing as you go, and whip finish.
Trim the head, starting underneath, then the sides and top. Snip carefully into the back edge so the collar of tips appears.

name: No Name Fly
description: A tiny pinfry imitation: flat pearl tinsel body, a small grizzly fibre wing and a modest built-up head with painted eyes.
fishing_tips: When trout are busting pinfry, cast into the activity on a long fluorocarbon leader and do nothing. The line tightens as the fly sinks.
imitates: Pinfry (newly hatched perch or roach fry)
hatch: Mid-summer to early autumn when pinfry shoal in the margins
mats: Small bunch of grizzly hackle fibres
steps: Lay a thread base and tie in the flat pearl tinsel.
Wind a smooth pearl body to just behind the eye and tie off.
Tie in a small bunch of grizzly hackle fibres as a wing.
Build a small (not too big) thread head, varnish it and paint on eyes.

name: One-Up Mayfly
creator_name: Phil White, Derbyshire Wye river keeper (Flydresser Spring 2004)
description: A hackleless mayfly that lies on its side with one elk wing flat on the water, like a dun caught in the film. Black pheasant tail tail and butt, ivory squirrel body, blue dun elk wings with a few moose fibres.
fishing_tips: Dress it sparse for rivers and fuller for lakes; it has done very well on the Irish loughs. A yellow-olive version (the Blown-Over Dun) is worth carrying too.
imitates: Mayfly (Ephemera danica) dun trapped on its side, or a spent spinner
hatch: Late May to mid-June, afternoons and evenings
mats: 3–4 dark cock pheasant tail fibres (melanistic or dyed black)
Blue dun dyed elk with a few moose fibres
Soft ivory dubbing (bleached fox squirrel or cream rabbit)
steps: Lay a solid thread base so the bulky wing can't spin around the shank.
Stack a bunch of elk hair, tie it in securely toward the front and trim the butts to a taper.
Tie in three or four dark pheasant tail fibres as the tail, leaving the butts long to wrap as a butt.
Wrap the butts as a small butt, then dub a slim ivory body to just short of the wing.
Stand the wing up and split it so one wing lies in the same plane as the body; the fly will sit with its body and one wing in the film.
Dub over the wing wraps for a thorax, clip the underside so it sits down, and whip finish.

name: Pearly Cormorant
creator_name: Pat Camber, Bewl Water (Fly Dressers' Guild Pattern Library)
description: The Cormorant with a shiny body: three layers of pearl Mylar ribbed with silver wire, a sparse black marabou wing and small jungle cock cheeks.
fishing_tips: A Bewl Water favourite on a washing-line or buzzer rig. Keep the wing to 12–15 fibres. Use orange goose biots if you don't have jungle cock.
imitates: Chironomid pupa (buzzer) or small fry
hatch: Through the season on stillwaters, especially during buzzer hatches
mats: Small jungle cock (or orange goose biots)
steps: Start the thread at the eye and run it back to just past the start of the bend. Tie in the wire.
Tie in the pearl Mylar and wind it forward, back and forward again in touching turns to build three smooth layers, stopping short of the eye.
Rib forward in open turns the opposite way to the Mylar.
Tie in a sparse black marabou wing just behind the eye, reaching a little past the bend. Trim the butts at an angle.
Add a small jungle cock cheek on each side, neaten the head, whip finish and varnish.

name: Rainy Day Spider
description: A semi-realistic wolf spider (Lycosidae) from Patagonia, where it's active in wet weather: a furry foam body over a black foam hump, suede chenille legs and palps bent with a hot needle, and marker spots.
fishing_tips: Fish it dry next to overhanging bushes and trees and let it land with a loud plop. Change colours to match local spiders.
imitates: Wolf spider (family Lycosidae) fallen onto the water
hatch: Summer and early autumn, especially in wet weather when spiders are washed or blown in
steps: Cover the shank with thread. Tie in a 1.5cm strip of Furry Foam, furry side down, at the back so it cups upward.
Tie a narrower strip of black foam on top facing back, fold it forward and tie it down to make a hump.
Pull the Furry Foam over the hump to form the rear body and tie it down. Don't cut the excess.
Cut four 7cm pieces and one 2cm piece of suede chenille and singe the ends to a taper.
Turn the hook over and tie the four long pieces side by side underneath, just in front of the rear body, centred so both sides match. Tie the short piece behind the eye for the palps.
Turn the hook upright, pull the Furry Foam over the legs and tie it off at the front.
Bend the legs up and add joints with a warm needle, point the palps forward, and dot the body and leg joints with a fine marker.

name: Robjent's Daddy
creator_name: Alistair Robjent, Stockbridge (shown by Ian McKenzie, Flydresser Spring 2021)
description: The chalkstream daddy sold by the jarful in Stockbridge: a foam underbody wrapped with peacock herl, knotted pheasant tail legs, hackle-tip wings and a dense red-brown cock hackle. A proven One Fly Competition fly on the Test.
fishing_tips: Fish it dry on rivers and lakes from late summer, when crane flies are blown onto the water.
imitates: Crane fly (daddy-long-legs, Tipulidae), adult on the surface
hatch: Late July to October, peaking in September on breezy days
mats: Knotted pheasant tail, four each side
steps: Take the thread to above the barb and tie in a 3–4mm strip of foam (any colour; it won't show).
Wrap the foam forward in slightly overlapping turns to make a tapered body.
Return the thread to the rear, tie in four peacock herls, twist them around the thread for strength and wind them over the foam in touching turns.
Tie in four knotted pheasant tail legs on each side.
Lay two cock hackles flat along the body and tie them in (they turn 90° as you wind), then tie in two hackle points as wings.
Wind several hackle turns behind the wings and a few in front. Whip finish and add a drop of varnish.

name: Rolled Wing Olive
description: A traditional dry olive from before split wings took over: dun fibre tail, stripped quill body and a single rolled (folded) wing of starling, teal or grey duck quill, with a few turns of dun hackle.
fishing_tips: Fish it to rising trout during olive hatches. Squeezed, the rolled wing collapses into the old 'crossbill' shape, which fish don't mind at all.
imitates: Olive dun (Baetidae, e.g. large dark olive or medium olive)
hatch: Large dark olives March–May and again in autumn; medium olives May–September; best on mild, damp days
mats: Starling (#14–18), teal (#14–16) or grey duck (#12–14) quill slip, rolled
steps: Lay a thread base and tie in a few dun fibres as the tail.
Tie in a stripped quill and wind a smooth, segmented body to about two-thirds of the shank.
Choose a wing quill to suit the hook size. Stroke a section of fibres out square to the stem so the tips line up.
Fold a quarter of the width inward (shiny side out), fold the other edge in the same way, then fold both doubles together so four layers make one wing.
Set the wing with the butts over the eye using a pinch-and-loop wrap, and trim the butts carefully with fine pliers while supporting the wing.
Wind four or five turns of hackle, two behind and two in front of the wing base, and whip finish.

name: Sawyer Pheasant Tail Nymph
creator_name: Frank Sawyer (Malcolm Price, Fly Dressers' Guild Pattern Library)
description: Frank Sawyer's original, tied with fine copper wire instead of thread: a pheasant tail tail, body and double-layered wing case over a copper thorax hump. In different sizes it passes for a dozen kinds of nymph.
fishing_tips: Cast upstream to sighted fish on clear rivers and let it sink, then lift it gently in front of the trout (the 'induced take').
imitates: Olive and other swimming mayfly nymphs (Baetidae)
hatch: All season on rivers; most useful from April to October
mats: Four long red-brown cock pheasant tail fibres
steps: Cover the shank evenly with copper wire from bend to eye and lock it so it can't spin.
Wind the wire back to just ahead of mid-shank and build a hump for the thorax, then take it to the bend.
Tie in four pheasant tail fibres by the tips so about ⅛ inch sticks out as a tail.
Twist the fibres with the wire for strength and wind them together in touching turns to the eye.
Separate the fibres from the wire and take the wire back in open turns to just behind the thorax.
Fold the fibres back over the thorax and secure them, then bring the wire forward and fold them forward again for a second layer.
Tie off at the eye with half a dozen turns of wire, trim and break off the wire. The thorax should bulge and the body taper to the tail.

name: Silver Doctor (trout size)
description: A miniature Silver Doctor in the old Ray Bergman style that crosses over from salmon to sea trout and brown trout: red wool butt, silver body, topping tail, blue hackle, grey mallard underwing and married blue, yellow and red goose sides.
fishing_tips: Try it on hard days on big reservoirs when nothing else works, especially when fry are about. It's an attractor, not an imitation.
imitates: Attractor; suggests small fry
hatch: Most effective mid-summer to autumn when fry are present
mats: Red, then black for the head
Married blue, yellow and red goose shoulder
steps: Lay a thread base and tie in a golden pheasant topping as the tail.
Make a short butt of red wool at the tail.
Tie in the oval rib and the flat silver tinsel at their separate points, wind a smooth silver body and rib it.
Wind a soft blue hackle and sweep it back.
Seat a pair of grey mallard slips firmly as the underwing (the sides won't sit well without it).
Marry thin strips of blue, yellow and red goose shoulder and tie one slab on each side. Trim any ragged tips.
Add small jungle cock cheeks if you like, form a black head and varnish.

name: Simple Beetle
description: A black foam beetle with a looped foam body and shellback, a dense cream rear hackle and a brown front hackle. Floats all day.
fishing_tips: A searching dry when nothing is showing. Fish it under trees and along edges where land insects fall in; it took four fish off the top in December when they ignored wets.
imitates: Terrestrial beetle (Coleoptera) fallen onto the water
hatch: Spring through autumn, especially warm, breezy days near trees and bankside cover
steps: Lay a thread base. Cut a 4mm foam strip with a pointed end.
Tie it in by the point halfway down the shank, bind it to the bend and bring the thread back.
Make a loop in the foam with a needle, bring the top part forward and tie it down two-thirds of the way along the shank.
Tie in a cream hackle behind the loose foam end and wind touching turns for a dense hackle. Tie off.
Tie in a brown hackle in front of the foam and wind three or four turns.
Pull the loose foam over the top and secure it at the head. Trim once it sits right and whip finish.

name: Grafham Shrimp
description: A simple freshwater shrimp: grey partridge tail and whisks, a spiky hare's ear body segmented with gold tinsel, a clear polythene shellback and a mono over-rib. Add a dark bead or lead for weight.
fishing_tips: Made for Grafham. Best as a dropper behind a weighted nymph, fished tight to stones and dam walls; shrimp feeders are often in water just inches deep.
imitates: Freshwater shrimp (Gammarus)
hatch: All year; especially important in colder months and in clear, weedy or rocky water
mats: Hare's ear or other spiky dubbing
Black or dark red bead, or lead wire (optional)
steps: Lay thread halfway down the bend and tie in a bunch of grey partridge fibres for the tail.
Tie in the mono over-rib, then the polythene shellback and the gold under-rib at the same point.
Take the thread forward, tie in a few more partridge fibres as head whisks, and return to the rear.
Dub a fairly heavy body and wind the gold rib in 8–9 tight open turns for segments.
Pull the shellback over and secure it at the head.
Wind the mono over the back, following the tinsel turns. Trim only when the shellback sits evenly, then whip finish and brush out the body for legs.

name: BWO Funneldun
description: Neil Patterson's Funneldun method: the hackle is funnelled forward over a thorax and V-cut on top, so the fly lands hook-up with the point hidden from the trout. The BWO mixes hot orange through blue dun hackle, a colour mix that suggests movement and evening light through the wings.
fishing_tips: Fish it to evening rises during the blue-winged olive hatch. The Funneldun method works for any hackled dry: match the colours to the hatch.
imitates: Blue-winged olive dun (Serratella ignita)
hatch: June to September, mostly in the evening on rivers
mats: Light fur (hare, rabbit or mink underfur)
Blue dun and hot orange cock, one size larger than the hook
steps: Dub a small thorax at the eye, about a third of the way down the shank.
Tie in the hackles behind the thorax facing backward, so the fibres slope forward.
Wind four or five turns of the mixed hackles, then wrap thread over the roots to push the fibres forward into a funnel at about 45°, supported by the thorax. Cover the thread with a little dubbing.
Tie in the tail a little way round the bend (not too far) and put a turn of thread under it to splay the fibres.
Dub a slim body back to the tail and tie off there.
Clip a small V out of the top of the hackle. The tail and funnelled hackle make the fly roll over and land hook-point up.

name: Skating Caddis
description: A small fluttering caddis: a ragged polypropylene shuck that props up the tail, a pheasant tail body locked with gold wire, a mink guard hair wing and a short-fibred blue dun or red hackle you can skate.
fishing_tips: Tie it small (no bigger than #14); there are lots of tiny caddis. Skate the full-hackled version, and trim the underside at the water if fish want it lower in the film.
imitates: Small caddis (sedge) adult hatching and fluttering on the surface
hatch: May to September, especially evenings and warm afternoons
mats: About five cock pheasant tail fibres
Short-fibred blue dun or red cock
steps: Tie in a small bunch of crinkly poly yarn as a ragged trailing shuck.
Tie in about five pheasant tail fibres and the gold wire.
Wrap the fibres forward to two-thirds of the shank, then rib the opposite way to lock them.
Pull the underfur out of a pinch of mink, stack the guard hairs and tie them in on top, extending past the bend. One lasso turn under the wing keeps it from splaying.
Wind a short-fibred hackle in close, non-overlapping turns, secure it and whip finish.

name: Surface Film Soldier Beetle
creator_name: Alan Middleton (Fly Dressers' Guild Pattern Library)
description: The simplest soldier beetle: a black thread underbody wrapped with bright orange wool and a short wing of black elk or moose hair, clipped to stubs at the front.
fishing_tips: Fish it in the film near flowering bankside plants on warm summer days.
imitates: Soldier beetle (Rhagonycha fulva) fallen onto the water
hatch: Mid-June to August, warm sunny days near hogweed, cow parsley and bankside flowers
mats: Black-dyed elk, deer or moose hair
steps: Form a black thread underbody.
Tie in and wrap a single strand of bright orange wool as the body.
Tie in a small bunch of black elk hair at the head as a wing.
Whip finish over the tie-in point and clip the butts to short stubs facing forward.

name: Sub-Surface Soldier Beetle
creator_name: Alan Middleton (Fly Dressers' Guild Pattern Library)
description: A sinking soldier beetle: tapered orange wool body, black hackle and a black feather wing case.
fishing_tips: Fish it just under the surface when beetles have drowned, or after the floaters are refused.
imitates: Drowned soldier beetle (Rhagonycha fulva)
hatch: Mid-June to August, warm sunny days near hogweed, cow parsley and bankside flowers
steps: At the tail, tie in orange wool, a black hackle and a bunch of black feather fibres.
Wrap the wool forward into a tapered body.
Wind the hackle forward and tie it off at the head.
Pull the feather fibres over the top as a wing case, tie them down at the head and whip finish.

name: Floating Soldier Palmer Beetle
creator_name: Alan Middleton (Fly Dressers' Guild Pattern Library)
description: An orange wool body palmered with a long black cock hackle, ribbed with the thread tag so the hackle stays put.
fishing_tips: Fish it dry in summer when soldier beetles are about; the palmered hackle keeps it riding high.
imitates: Soldier beetle (Rhagonycha fulva) fallen onto the water
hatch: Mid-June to August, warm sunny days near hogweed, cow parsley and bankside flowers
steps: Form a black thread underbody, leaving the tag end hanging at the tail.
Tie in orange wool at the tail and wrap a tapered body.
Tie in a long black hackle at the head and palmer it back to the end of the body.
Use the thread tag as a rib: trap the hackle and wind it forward the opposite way without catching fibres. Whip finish at the head.

name: Soldier Palmer (Orange Variant)
description: A sparse orange palmer with a hot orange fluorescent tail, orange seal's fur body, fine gold rib and a light red or ginger hackle. Half of the 'Tadpole Team' with a Black Tadpole.
fishing_tips: Fish it on the dropper five or six feet above a Black Tadpole. With a little lead in the body it works slow and deep on small stillwaters.
imitates: Attractor; suggests a hatching sedge or a beetle
hatch: All season; especially effective summer into autumn
mats: Extra-fine oval gold tinsel or fine gold wire
Natural light red or ginger cock, not too short
steps: Tie in a short tail of hot orange fluorescent floss and the gold rib.
Dub an orange seal's fur body and tie in the hackle at the front.
Palmer the hackle back to the bend in open turns (it doesn't need to be bushy; this fly should sink) and trap it with two turns of the rib.
Wind the rib forward through the hackle, keeping it at right angles to the shank and tight, so you don't drag fibres down.
Tie off at the head and whip finish.

name: Supersized Zulu
description: The classic Zulu scaled up for salmon: red wool tail, black seal's fur body, oval silver rib, two black cock hackles palmered for a bushy outline and a black hen collar.
fishing_tips: Supersized loch flies for salmon in a spate-river-fed Scottish loch. Fish them bushy and on the move to create a disturbance; tied small, they're the classic trout patterns.
mats: Two black cock neck hackles (Whiting Bronze grade)
steps: Lay a thread base and tie in a short red wool tail and the oval silver rib.
Dub a black seal's fur body, leaving room at the head.
Tie in two black cock hackles at the front and palmer them together back to the tail (about eight turns gives a bushy fly).
Trap the hackles with the rib and wind it forward through them to the head.
Wind a large soft black hen hackle as a collar, form the head and whip finish.

name: Supersized Golden Olive Bumble
description: Kingsmill Moore's Golden Olive Bumble scaled up for salmon: topping tail, golden olive seal's fur body, gold rib, two palmered golden olive hackles and a collar of blue guinea fowl over golden pheasant yellow rump.
fishing_tips: Supersized loch flies for salmon in a spate-river-fed Scottish loch. Fish them bushy and on the move to create a disturbance; tied small, they're the classic trout patterns.
mats: Golden pheasant yellow rump feather, then blue guinea fowl
steps: Tie in a golden pheasant topping tail and the oval gold rib.
Dub a golden olive seal's fur body.
Palmer two golden olive hackles from the front back to the tail and lock them with the rib, winding it forward through them.
Wind a golden pheasant yellow rump feather as a collar, then blue guinea fowl in front of it.
Form the head and whip finish.

name: Supersized Peter Ross
description: The Fly Dressers' Guild emblem fly, scaled up: topping tail, silver rear body and scarlet seal's fur front, oval silver rib, black hen collar and (because teal doesn't come that long) a grey squirrel wing.
fishing_tips: Supersized loch flies for salmon in a spate-river-fed Scottish loch. Fish them bushy and on the move to create a disturbance; tied small, they're the classic trout patterns.
mats: Natural grey squirrel (teal on small sizes)
steps: Tie in a topping tail and the oval silver rib.
Wind the rear half of the body in flat silver tinsel, then dub the front half in scarlet seal's fur. Rib the whole body.
Take a wrap of thread around a bunch of grey squirrel before setting it on top; it stops the hair rolling down the side. Tie it in as the wing.
Trim the butts short and seal them with a drop of varnish.
Add a black hen beard or collar, form a neat head and whip finish.

name: Supersized Alexandra
description: The once-banned Alexandra, scaled up: red goose tail and cheeks, silver body with oval silver rib, a wing of peacock sword from matched left and right feathers, and a black hen collar.
fishing_tips: Supersized loch flies for salmon in a spate-river-fed Scottish loch. Fish them bushy and on the move to create a disturbance; tied small, they're the classic trout patterns. The Alexandra is a strong fry imitation for trout.
mats: Pair of red goose shoulder slips
steps: Tie in a pair of red goose slips as the tail and the oval silver rib.
Wind a smooth silver body and rib it.
Match a left and a right peacock sword feather, take an equal number of fibres from each and tie them in one side at a time so they don't roll.
Add a red goose slip on each side as cheeks.
Wind a black hen collar, form the head and whip finish.

name: Teeny Nymph
description: Jim Teeny's all-pheasant-tail nymph: two tapered sections of wrapped pheasant tail, each with its butt-heavy shoulder and the tips drawn down as legs. Tied in many colours, from natural for lake trout to bright for Pacific salmon and steelhead.
fishing_tips: Jim fishes it in every size and colour for trout, steelhead and salmon, controlling depth so the fly is right in the fish's face. Bright colours are for the Pacific coast and Alaska.
imitates: General nymph or scud (shrimp); a suggestive pattern
hatch: All season in lakes and rivers; also used for migratory fish runs
mats: Nymph or wet hook (e.g. Kamasan B175, Mustad R90), #2–14
Cock pheasant tail fibres (natural or dyed)
steps: Lay a thread base from mid-shank to the bend.
Do a trial run: tie in a few pheasant tail fibres by the butts and wrap them to mid-shank to check the leg length for your hook.
Tie in a sizeable bunch of fibres by the butts at the bend and trim the waste to a taper.
Wrap them forward to mid-shank so the section is thickest at the rear, with a definite shoulder. Secure them.
Pull the tips down under the shank as legs and set them with a few turns, sloping slightly back.
Repeat the whole process for the front section, then draw the tips down as a second set of legs. Varnish the head.
