name: Terry's Terror
creator_name: Dr Cecil Terry and Ernest Lock (Geoff Hill, Flydresser Winter 2007)
description: A dry fly from the Orange Tag family: a tag of hot orange and yellow cock fibres, a peacock herl body with a broad flat gold rib and a deep red cock hackle trimmed short underneath so it sits in the film.
fishing_tips: A great searching dry that brings trout and grayling up when nothing is rising. On #16–18 it's an everyday dry; on #14 it covers early-season large dark olives; on #12 it passes for a sedge.
imitates: General dry: olive dun (small sizes) or sedge (large sizes)
hatch: All season on rivers; large dark olives in March–April, sedges on summer evenings
mats: Cock fibres dyed hot orange, with a smaller bunch dyed yellow
Deep red cock (gamecock if you have it), trimmed underneath
steps: Tie in a bunch of orange cock fibres with a smaller bunch of yellow, points toward the eye. Cut the butts short and fold the tips back so the tag projects past the bend.
Tie in the flat gold tinsel and two or three peacock herls together.
Wind the herl body forward, then rib it with the gold in open turns.
Tie in a good red cock hackle and wind it, then tie off.
Trim the hackle fibres under the shank short, spinner-style, so the fly sits in the film. Whip finish.

name: Big Red
creator_name: Bill Latham and the Bath & District team (Ian McKenzie, Flydresser Winter 2020)
description: A Shipman's Buzzer with a parachute: a finely dubbed red seal's fur body with wire rib, white poly breathers and a post pulled forward over a soft parachute hackle. It's a stuck, crippled midge.
fishing_tips: Grease the hackle and breathers but let the tail dip below the surface. Use a visible dry on the dropper as a sighter and watch for swirls. A Bristol reservoirs, Rutland, Grafham and Draycote staple; tie other colours on #12–16.
imitates: Chironomid midge emerging, crippled and stuck in the surface film
hatch: Spring to autumn on stillwaters; big red midges in early season, other colours through summer
mats: Kamasan B170 or similar, #10 (#12–16 for other colours)
White polypropylene or Glo-Brite multi yarn
Soft cock or natural furnace hen
steps: Run the thread to above the barb. Tie in the poly yarn leaving a short tail, bind it toward the eye, stopping 2–3mm short, then stand it up and wrap around its base for a post.
Tie in the hackle by the tip at the post (not too stiff a cock hackle) and run the thread back to the tail, tying in the wire as you go.
Dub a fine seal's fur body forward to the post and rib it in open turns, tying off in front of the post.
Wind five or six turns of hackle around the post and tie down.
Take one turn of dubbing in front of the post, pull the post forward and tie it down at the eye. Whip finish and trim the breathers to length.

name: The Carson
creator_name: Irish lough pattern via Norman Wells (Chris Reeves, Flydresser Summer 2024)
description: A heavily dressed Irish lough fly: orange and bronze mallard tail, golden olive seal's fur body with a palmered golden olive hackle, an orange hen shoulder, a bronze mallard wing and a front hackle of golden olive mallard flank.
fishing_tips: Short-lined as the top dropper in a team of three from a drifting boat in a big wave. It's built to stick in the film when you dibble it.
imitates: Hatching sedge or general lough insect life; an attractor
hatch: Summer on the loughs, especially in a good wave; mayfly and sedge time
mats: Orange cock fibres under bronze mallard
Fine oval gold tinsel or gold wire
Grey mallard flank dyed pale golden olive
steps: Lay a thread base. Tie in a bunch of orange cock fibres about as long as the shank, curving up, and bind the butts along the shank.
Tie a bunch of bronze mallard of equal length on top, then the rib, covering the waste for an even underbody.
Dub a tight golden olive seal's fur body.
Tie in the golden olive hackle at the head, wind it back in open turns, then rib forward through it. Trim.
Wind two turns of orange hen at the shoulder.
Tie in a small bunch of bronze mallard on top as the wing.
Wind two or three turns of golden olive mallard flank, stroking the fibres back. Form a neat head, whip finish and varnish.

name: Collared Undertaker
description: A Newfoundland twist on Warren Duncan's Undertaker: gold tag, green and red butt, peacock herl body ribbed gold, black calf tail wing and a black hen collar.
fishing_tips: Let it swing across the current naturally, just under the surface; a small upstream mend lifts it higher. Collared flies are Jamie's go-to when a customer just wants 'flies that work'.
mats: Hen saddle dyed black, three turns
steps: Lay a thread base and wind a short mylar tag above the hook point.
Build a small butt in front of the tag.
Tie in the oval French tinsel for the rib, then wind the body forward, leaving room at the head.
Rib the body in open, even turns and tie off.
Tie in a sparse wing on top, reaching about to the bend.
Wind the hen saddle collar two or three turns and sweep it back.
Form the head, whip finish and varnish.

name: Mini Green Cosseboom
description: A very small version of Winston's Green Cosseboom: silver tag, red butt, golden pheasant crest tail, green stretch-floss body ribbed silver, grey squirrel wing and a yellow hen collar. One of Jamie's best flies on the Humber in all conditions.
fishing_tips: Let it swing across the current naturally, just under the surface; a small upstream mend lifts it higher. Collared flies are Jamie's go-to when a customer just wants 'flies that work'.
mats: Hen saddle dyed yellow, two turns
steps: Lay a thread base and wind a short mylar tag above the hook point.
Tie in a golden pheasant crest as the tail.
Build a small butt in front of the tag.
Tie in the oval French tinsel for the rib, then wind the body forward, leaving room at the head.
Rib the body in open, even turns and tie off.
Tie in a sparse wing on top, reaching about to the bend.
Wind the hen saddle collar two or three turns and sweep it back.
Form the head, whip finish and varnish.

name: Besure
description: Robert Chaisson's season-long Atlantic salmon staple: silver tag, hot pink butt, Green Highlander yarn body ribbed silver, grey squirrel wing, Highlander green hen collar and a fluorescent head.
fishing_tips: Let it swing across the current naturally, just under the surface; a small upstream mend lifts it higher. Collared flies are Jamie's go-to when a customer just wants 'flies that work'.
mats: Hen saddle dyed Highlander green, two turns
steps: Lay a thread base and wind a short mylar tag above the hook point.
Build a small butt in front of the tag.
Tie in the oval French tinsel for the rib, then wind the body forward, leaving room at the head.
Rib the body in open, even turns and tie off.
Tie in a sparse wing on top, reaching about to the bend.
Wind the hen saddle collar two or three turns and sweep it back.
Form the head with fluorescent floss, whip finish and varnish.

name: Irritator (Newfoundland variant)
description: A Northern Peninsula fly, close to Quebec's Irritator: silver tag, black floss body ribbed silver, moose body hair wing and a white hen collar.
fishing_tips: Let it swing across the current naturally, just under the surface; a small upstream mend lifts it higher. Collared flies are Jamie's go-to when a customer just wants 'flies that work'.
steps: Lay a thread base and wind a short mylar tag above the hook point.
Tie in the oval French tinsel for the rib.
Wind the body forward, leaving room at the head.
Rib the body in open, even turns and tie off.
Tie in a sparse wing on top, reaching about to the bend.
Wind the hen saddle collar two or three turns and sweep it back.
Form the head, whip finish and varnish.

name: Corrigan (variant)
description: Bill Baker's Corrigan in streamer style with Jamie's additions: gold tag, fluorescent butt, hare's mask body ribbed gold, white calf tail wing, orange hen collar and a fluorescent orange head.
fishing_tips: Let it swing across the current naturally, just under the surface; a small upstream mend lifts it higher. Collared flies are Jamie's go-to when a customer just wants 'flies that work'. Jamie prefers the Corrigan in larger sizes late in the season.
mats: 3X long, 2X heavy nymph hook (e.g. Sprite S1200), #4–10
Hen saddle dyed orange, two or three turns
steps: Lay a thread base and wind a short mylar tag above the hook point.
Build a small butt in front of the tag.
Tie in the oval French tinsel for the rib, then wind the body forward, leaving room at the head.
Rib the body in open, even turns and tie off.
Tie in a sparse wing on top, reaching about to the bend.
Wind the hen saddle collar two or three turns and sweep it back.
Form the head with fluorescent orange floss, whip finish and varnish.

name: Tiger Nymph
creator_name: Flydresser, Spring 2004 (inspired by a Siberian tiger in British Columbia)
description: A buggy reddish-tan nymph: cree fibre tail, a slim cat-underfur abdomen ribbed with doubled black thread, a peacock herl wing case and two sets of pine squirrel guard hair legs.
fishing_tips: A general nymph for rivers and lakes; fish it dead-drift or with a slow hand-twist.
imitates: Mayfly or stonefly nymph (crawling or clinging types)
hatch: All season; most useful spring to early summer before hatches
mats: Short bunch of cree hackle fibres
Pine squirrel back guard hair, two bunches
steps: Run the thread down the shank and tie in a shortish bunch of cree fibres and a doubled length of black thread. Trim the butts at mid-shank and bind them level.
Dub a thin noodle of underfur and wrap a slender abdomen over the rear half. Rib it in even turns.
Tie in four or five peacock herls for the wing case.
Tie a small stacked bunch of pine squirrel guard hair on top at the same point, tips back over the abdomen, as the rear legs.
Dub a slightly heavier noodle and wrap part of the thorax, then tie in a second bunch of guard hair, a little longer, for the front legs.
Split each bunch of legs into two with your thumbnail, pull the herl forward over the thorax as a wing case and tie it down at the eye.
Trim the herl, form a neat head, whip finish and add head cement.

name: Ivens' March Brown
description: Tom Ivens' river variation of the Gold Ribbed Hare's Ear: two partridge fibre tails, a rough hare's ear body ribbed gold, a dark partridge collar and a bold peacock herl head.
fishing_tips: A general-purpose river wet. A little roughness adds to its appeal; it suggests olive nymphs, caddis, shrimp or emergers.
imitates: March brown nymph or emerger (Rhithrogena germanica); also a general olive nymph
hatch: March brown hatches March–May around midday on rivers; general use all season
mats: Hare's ear (or chopped rabbit or hare guard hair)
steps: Lay a thread base and tie in two speckled partridge fibres as tails, then the gold rib.
Dub a rough hare's ear body and rib it with the gold.
Wind a dark partridge hackle as a collar.
Twist a couple of peacock herls and wind a bold head in front of the hackle. Whip finish.

name: Ivens' Partridge & Orange
description: Tom Ivens' more nymph-like version of the North Country classic: an orange-dyed herl body ribbed with fine gold wire, a thicker thorax under an orange herl wing case and a long-fibred dark partridge collar.
fishing_tips: Fish it sparse in fast North Country streams for trout and grayling, and when the water is coloured after rain. It can pass for a February red, a spinner, a nymph or a shrimp. (Swan herl is protected; use dyed goose herl.)
imitates: February red stonefly (Taeniopteryx nebulosa), or a general nymph or spinner
hatch: February red: February–April on rivers; useful all season in coloured water
mats: Orange-dyed herl (goose in place of the original swan)
Dark partridge, fairly long in the fibre
steps: Tie in the gold wire and a few orange herls at the bend.
Wind a slim herl body to about two-thirds of the shank and rib it with the wire.
Tie in more orange herl on top for the wing case, then wind a thicker herl thorax.
Pull the wing case forward and tie it down.
Wind a sparse dark partridge collar, form a small head and varnish.

name: Trans Caddis
creator_name: Davy Wotton (tied by Chris Reeves, Flydresser Summer 2016)
description: A versatile caddis pupa and emerger: hare's ear body with ostrich herl and gold rib, a Swiss straw wing case, knotted pheasant tail legs, a tan CDC puff wing and a partridge hackle.
fishing_tips: On the top dropper during a caddis hatch, draw it up and dibble it just under the surface for splashy takes. Fished deeper as a swimming pupa, pause it; takes often come a few seconds after it stops. Use a finer rib and more dubbing for the emerger, a heavier hook and less dubbing for the pupa.
imitates: Caddis (sedge) pupa swimming up to hatch, and the emerging adult
hatch: May to September, especially evenings; caddis hatch all season on many rivers
mats: Wet or grub hook, #10–14 (heavier for fishing deep)
Two pairs of knotted pheasant tail fibres
steps: Tie in the wire and gold tinsel ribs and dub a hare's ear body.
Wind ostrich herl over the body, then counter-wrap the gold tinsel to protect it.
Shape a piece of Swiss straw and tie it on top as a wing case, keeping the head area clear.
Tie in two pairs of knotted pheasant tail legs, one pair each side.
Tie in a tan CDC puff as a wing, trimming the thick stem cleanly so it doesn't leave a lump.
Wind two turns of partridge or hen, folded back. Form a neat head and whip finish.

name: Turkey Mayfly Spinner
creator_name: Chris Reeves (Fly Dressers' Guild Pattern Library)
description: Chris Reeves' most effective spent mayfly: three moose tails, a black peacock butt, a flat white turkey herl body, white calf tail wings tied spent and a black hackle figure-eighted through the wing roots.
fishing_tips: Fish it in the evening fall of spent mayfly, flat in the film where trout are sipping dying spinners.
imitates: Mayfly spent spinner (Ephemera danica, the 'spent gnat')
hatch: Late May to mid-June, evening spinner falls
mats: Two turns of black-dyed peacock herl
Four white turkey herls, wound flat
White calf tail, split and tied spent
Black cock, a size small, about eight turns
steps: Stack a bunch of white calf tail and tie it in facing forward about 2mm back from the eye. Split it and figure-eight it into the spent position, each wing as long as the shank. Trim the waste at an angle and bind back to the tail.
Tie in three moose hairs, divided, about 1.5 times the body length.
Wind two turns of black peacock herl as a butt.
Wind four white turkey herls flat in touching turns to the wings (change hands so they don't twist) and tie off.
Tie in a long black hackle, a size small for the hook. Wind five or six turns behind the wings, figure-eight over each wing root, and finish with one turn at the eye.
Whip finish and varnish the knot.

name: Viva
creator_name: Victor Furze, early 1970s (Chris Reeves, Flydresser Autumn 2020)
description: The classic black-and-green stillwater lure: fluorescent green tail, black chenille body with four turns of silver, black marabou wing, often with jungle cock cheeks. The white version is the Wyvern.
fishing_tips: Fish it on a floating or intermediate line with a steady retrieve. Still a winner in competitions, traditional dressing and all.
imitates: Attractor lure; suggests a leech or small fish
hatch: All season, especially early and late in the year on stillwaters
steps: Lay a thread base and tie in a short fluorescent green tail.
Tie in the silver tinsel and the black chenille at the tail.
Wind the chenille body forward and rib it with four turns of silver.
Tie in a black marabou wing reaching past the tail.
Add jungle cock cheeks if you like, form the head and whip finish.

name: Yellow Dung Fly
description: A plump yellow chenille fly with a red cock hackle, a flat grey poly wing lying along the back and a big yellow thread head with marked eyes. Matched to the natural: 10mm body, 13mm wing.
fishing_tips: Fish it near the banks of grazed reservoirs and lakes, where dung flies are often blown onto the water; they can be about even in December.
imitates: Yellow dung fly (Scathophaga stercoraria), adult blown onto the water
hatch: Spring through autumn (and mild winter days) near livestock pasture and grassy banks
steps: Take the thread to the hook point, tie in the chenille core and continue to the bend, then bring the thread to mid-shank.
Wind the chenille to the thread for a plump body and tie in the cock hackle there.
Make two turns of hackle, tie off and trim.
Wind the chenille on toward the head, leaving 3mm clear behind the eye.
Build a large yellow thread head, then trim the chenille and hackle on top so the wing can lie flat.
Tie in a flat grey poly wing slightly behind the eye, trim the waste, finish building the head and mark the eyes with a brown pen.

name: 6-inch UV Pike Fly
description: A big-profile but light all-synthetic pike streamer. A half rubber bead behind the eye props up a short layer of Curly Creature Hair so a little material makes lots of volume; a curly dubbing head pushes water, with glow eyes under UV resin. It doesn't soak up water and lasts nearly a season.
fishing_tips: Fish it with discreet jerks and light strips just under the surface; it casts on a #6 rod. Natural colours most of the time, a bright one in winter. Put a little more material underneath for a keel, and brush it back into shape after each fish.
mats: Predator hook (e.g. Partridge Bad Boy Predator 4/0 or wide-gape 6/0)
6mm oval rubber bead, cut in half
Curly Creature Hair, black and pearl grey, with black holographic flash
Superglue (gel and liquid) and UV resin (medium, thin, flex fluo orange)
Hair straightener, hair clips, hollow tube, UV torch
steps: Cut the rubber bead in half and thread it on flat side toward the eye. Lay 1.5cm of thread behind the eye with a small bump at the end, glue it and push the bead onto the bump.
Take a pinch of body hair (about a toothpick's thickness for 6/0), cut it to 16–18cm and taper both ends by rolling and pulling.
Straighten about 10cm of one end and 3–4cm of the other with the hair straightener, just until the fibres change, then switch it off.
Tie the material in front of the bead, long end forward, two-thirds along its length. Spread it round the shank with a little more on top, then tighten.
Brush the fibres, flip the long ends back with a hollow tube so they cloak the short ones, and tie them down hard against the bead.
Add lateral scale on each side, clip everything back out of the way and wick liquid superglue into the wraps.
Cut head dubbing to about 1.3× the body length and tie it on top with two-thirds facing back. Turn the hook over and add a slightly shorter bunch underneath the same way. Glue the wraps.
Pluck the dubbing apart all round the shank and flip the forward fibres back with the tube. Make a few supporting wraps in front and whip finish.
Glue on the eyes and cover them with UV resin for a durable head.

name: Pulling Hopper
description: A slim hopper for pulling rather than static fishing: a sparse fiery red seal's fur body with a pearl rib, two pairs of knotted legs pointing down and just three or four turns of webby Indian cock hackle.
fishing_tips: Pull it through the surface layer on a floating or midge-tip line. Keep the dubbing and the hackle sparse so the stray seal's fur gives it life.
imitates: Hatching midge or sedge and terrestrials; a reservoir 'hopper' suggestion
hatch: Summer on stillwaters, especially in a ripple
mats: Red or to match the body
Seal's fur, blend with plenty of fiery red fluorescent fibres
Two sets of knotted pheasant tail, knots 5–6mm from the tips
steps: Lay a thread base and tie in the pearl rib.
Dub the thread very lightly with seal's fur and wind a slender body to just short of the eye.
Rib forward in open turns, leaving plenty of dubbing showing between them.
Tie a set of knotted legs on each side, tips pointing down, and check their alignment.
Make only three or four turns of a webby cock hackle; more would kill the action.
Make a small head, sweep the hackle back, leave the eye clear and whip finish.
